title: 2 Chronicles 20:31–37
context: 2 Chronicles 20:31–37 closes the account of Jehoshaphat’s reign and parallels 1 Kings 22:41–49. The age, length of reign, and mother’s name match Kings. Differences are named rather than harmonized: Chronicles says that “the people had still not set their hearts on the God of their fathers” (20:33), where Kings says “The people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.”; Chronicles cites “the history of Jehu the son of Hanani” (20:34), where Kings cites “the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah”. Chronicles then says that Jehoshaphat joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel to make ships “to go to Tarshish” at Ezion Geber, and that the ships were wrecked after Eliezer son of Dodavahu prophesied against the alliance (20:35–37). Kings says “Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold”, that they wrecked at Ezion Geber, and that when Ahaziah asked to send his servants, “But Jehoshaphat would not.” (1 Kings 22:48–49). As the notes on 1 Kings 22:48–49 say, the relationship between the two accounts is discussed by interpreters and left unresolved here. The apparent tension between 17:6 and 20:33 about the high places is also left open. Both traditions read the section as shared ground: Jehoshaphat was a faithful king whose alliances with Ahab’s house brought real loss.

verses.text: So Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign. He reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat reigns over Judah; he is thirty-five when he begins to reign and reigns twenty-five years in Jerusalem, and his mother is Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. The figures match 1 Kings 22:42.

Arminian readers note the long and stable reign and see the summary as recording a life of real faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness in giving Judah a lasting reign under a king who sought him, and they note that the naming of the queen mother is a regular feature of Judah’s royal records.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:42, and read the summary as the closing frame of Jehoshaphat’s story.

verses.text: He walked in the way of Asa his father, and didn’t turn away from it, doing that which was right in the LORD’s eyes.
verses.arminianNotes:
He walks in the way of Asa his father and does not turn away from it, doing what is right in the LORD’s eyes. Kings has “He walked in all the way of Asa his father.”

Arminian readers note the honest assessment of a king who remained faithful in the main direction of his life, and they see this as an encouragement that real faithfulness is possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a godly king whose reforms were genuine, and they note that the evaluation is given despite the failures the Chronicler has recorded, which shows God’s gracious judgment of his servant.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:43, and record the small wording difference from Kings.

verses.text: However the high places were not taken away, and the people had still not set their hearts on the God of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes:
However, the high places are not taken away, and the people have still not set their hearts on the God of their fathers. Kings says instead that the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.

Arminian readers note that reform at the top does not guarantee change in every heart, and they see each person responsible to set the heart on God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the verse stands in tension with 17:6, where Jehoshaphat took away the high places, and they leave the relationship between the two statements open, as the notes on 1 Kings 22:43 do.

Both traditions read the verse as an honest admission that the people’s hearts were not fully turned, and they treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last, behold, they are written in the history of Jehu the son of Hanani, which is included in the book of the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Jehoshaphat’s acts, first and last, are written in the history of Jehu the son of Hanani, which is included in the book of the kings of Israel. Kings cites the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah instead.

Arminian readers note that the prophet who rebuked Jehoshaphat in 19:2 is also named as the recorder of his reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the prophetic record of the king’s reign as part of God’s providential preservation of history, and they note that the identity of this Jehu with the earlier figures of the same name is discussed.

Both traditions treat the source citation as shared ground and record the difference from Kings without trying to reconstruct the sources.

verses.text: After this, Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel. The same did very wickedly.
verses.arminianNotes:
After this, Jehoshaphat king of Judah joins himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who does very wickedly. Another alliance with Ahab’s house follows.

Arminian readers note that Jehoshaphat repeats the kind of partnership Jehu had rebuked, and they see this as a sober warning that the lessons of one failure can be forgotten through later free choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the verse a pattern of weakness in a godly king, and they note that Chronicles’ account of this alliance seems to differ from 1 Kings 22:49, where Jehoshaphat refuses Ahaziah’s request; as the notes on 1 Kings 22:49 say, this is left unresolved.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the danger of ungodly alliances.

verses.text: He joined himself with him to make ships to go to Tarshish. They made the ships in Ezion Geber.
verses.arminianNotes:
He joins with Ahaziah to make ships to go to Tarshish, and they make the ships in Ezion Geber. Kings speaks of “ships of Tarshish” to go to Ophir for gold (1 Kings 22:48).

Arminian readers see a commercial venture undertaken in partnership, and they note that the text treats the partnership itself as the problem rather than trade as such.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Ezion Geber lay “beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea” (1 Kings 9:26), and that the location of Tarshish is uncertain, so the relation between the destinations in Kings and Chronicles is discussed and left open.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and record the differences from Kings without harmonizing them.

verses.text: Then Eliezer the son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, “Because you have joined yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” The ships were wrecked, so that they were not able to go to Tarshish.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesies against Jehoshaphat, “Because you have joined yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” The ships are wrecked and cannot go to Tarshish. Kings reports the wreck without a prophecy (1 Kings 22:48).

Arminian readers see a clear consequence attached to a free choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s fatherly discipline of a king he loved, and they note that the account ends Jehoshaphat’s story with a reminder of 19:2. The relationship with 1 Kings 22:48–49 is left unresolved, consistent with the notes there.

Both traditions read the verse soberly as shared ground: alliances with those who do wickedly bring loss, even for a faithful king.
